title: Friday’s relief meets weekend risk.
deck: My read: stronger stocks did not remove the tension between expensive capital and fragile consumer expectations. Weekend diplomacy adds a fresh uncertainty for the next session—not an explanation of Friday’s close. Test the cash-flow impact separately from the discount-rate impact.

sections.title: Stocks recovered; the yield curve gave a mixed signal.
sections.body: Friday’s S&P 500 rose 0.5%, the Dow 0.9% and the Nasdaq Composite 0.5%, according to AP. Treasury’s daily par yields were 4.81% at two years, 5.17% at ten years and 5.49% at thirty years: changes of −6, −1 and +2 basis points from Thursday. The 10Y–2Y spread widened to 36 basis points from 31. My interpretation: this was not uniform relief across borrowing maturities. A slightly lower ten-year yield alone is weak evidence that the longer-term valuation hurdle has eased. Nominal yields cannot tell us how much came from real rates, inflation compensation or term premium.

sections.title: Weaker confidence and higher expected inflation complicate the story.
sections.body: Michigan’s final September sentiment index fell to 48.1 from 51.7 in August—a 3.6-point decline. Year-ahead inflation expectations increased to 4.6% from 4.0%; long-run expectations edged to 3.4% from 3.3%. These are survey expectations, not measured inflation or a Federal Reserve forecast. My assessment: businesses could face customers who resist discretionary spending while still expecting higher prices. That is a potential margin problem, not proof of an imminent recession. The counterargument is that gloomy attitudes do not translate mechanically into weaker purchases. Subsequent spending, unit volumes and company guidance would be better tests of whether confidence is becoming a cash-flow problem.

sections.title: Do not price a reopening as a settled outcome.
sections.body: Reuters reported on Sunday that Trump had said Saturday he rejected Iran’s proposal to reopen Hormuz and end fighting. Iran continued to seek diplomacy and said mediators had not formally conveyed a US rejection. My inference: near-term supply normalization remains uncertain, but negotiations are not demonstrably over. This development occurred after Friday’s cash-market close; it cannot explain that session’s returns, and Monday’s response has not occurred at this cutoff. The relevant business question is how persistent transport and energy costs might affect margins and working capital. A negotiated reopening would weaken that concern; a headline alone does not establish either the duration or magnitude of the cost shock.

sections.title: Use separate operating and valuation scenarios.
sections.body: For a DCF, compare a normalization case with a persistent-cost case. In the latter, test weaker cash-flow growth or a lower normalized starting free cash flow, then vary WACC separately. Do not mechanically add consumer inflation expectations to WACC, or treat Treasury par yields as a company’s full cost of capital. An energy producer and a fuel-intensive operator can have very different exposures to the same headline. The toolkit’s constant-growth model is a simplified sensitivity exercise: temporary disruptions need an explicit year-by-year model to distinguish recovery timing from permanent damage. The useful output is a range with transparent assumptions, not a precise price target.

watch: Look for confirmed changes in shipping access and negotiating terms. Separate announcements from demonstrated normalization; do not assume the next market reaction in advance.
Compare future consumer spending and company volume/margin evidence with the survey’s weaker outlook. Resilient purchasing would challenge the demand-warning interpretation.
Watch whether any easing in short-maturity yields extends to longer maturities. A sustained decline without deteriorating cash flows would soften the valuation headwind.
caveat: Codex’s analysis, not Owen’s personal view or investment advice. Equity closes and Treasury observations cover Friday 25 September, the latest completed US cash session. Research cutoff is Sunday 27 September at the displayed ET/HKT time; this is not a live quote feed. Weekend news is explicitly separate from Friday’s market performance. Index percentage changes are rounded. Treasury figures are daily par yields, not executable quotes. Michigan figures are final September survey results; expectations are not realized inflation. Geopolitical reporting remains subject to new statements and developments. Interpretations are conditional, and co-movement does not establish causation.
